subtype: Approach: tracking where time actually goes for a week [Thinking]
passage: For a week I kept a tally on a sticky note stuck to my monitor. Every time I answered a work message after six, I made a tick; every late meeting, a dash; every real emergency, a star. I had been feeling guilty all month, sure I was always behind. By Friday the note told a different story: forty-one ticks, six dashes, one star. Nearly all my late hours were replies to chat pings that could have waited. The one star was a failing build that Pema and I fixed together. Seeing the numbers, the vague guilt shrank into something I could work with. I can decide about pings. I cannot decide about a broken build. - Gargi

qa.q: How many real emergencies did Gargi count in the week?
qa.a: Gargi counted one, the failing build.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel about work before keeping the tally?
qa.a: Gargi felt guilty and sure of always being behind.

qa.q: What could Gargi try next, based on the tally?
qa.a: Gargi could check chats at set times in the evening instead of answering each ping, and agree with colleagues how to flag a real emergency.

qa.q: How might Pema see the tally?
qa.a: Pema, who helped fix the build, may see the emergency as real but rare, and may welcome clearer signals about what is urgent.

grounding: Gargi logs a week of late messages, meetings and emergencies, and finds most late work was replying to chats.

subtype: Approach: tracking where time actually goes for a week [Thinking]
passage:
Mentoring note, Friday.
Harsha came to our one-to-one with a printed sheet instead of the usual apology for looking tired. For seven days he had jotted down every work chat, every meeting and every evening hour in a notebook column. He walked me through it aloud: "I thought the late nights were because of outages. Look, only two entries after nine were real incidents. The other nineteen were me answering chat pings that could have waited till morning." He tapped the tally. "So I don't need to feel bad about being slow. I need to stop treating every ping as a fire."
I asked what he would test next week. He said he would mute the team chat after eight and check it once. I have booked a follow-up in two weeks to look at his next sheet.
— Sarika

qa.q: How many entries after nine were real incidents?
qa.a: Only two entries after nine were real incidents; the other nineteen were chat pings that could have waited till morning.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling about the late nights before the log, and what changed?
qa.a: Harsha had been carrying a vague guilt about being slow and tired; the tally left him relieved and clearer, because the real problem was a habit of answering pings.

qa.q: What else could Harsha pair with the log to make the change stick?
qa.a: He could add an if-then rule, such as checking the muted chat once at eight and leaving anything that is not an incident for the morning.

qa.q: How might Harsha's teammates be affected when he stops replying at night?
qa.a: At first they may wait a little longer for answers, but they can learn to flag true incidents clearly, and his morning replies will likely be sharper.

grounding: It shows an engineer tracking a week of chats, meetings and evening hours and finding that most late work is chat replies, so data replaces vague guilt.

subtype: Approach: tracking where time actually goes for a week [Thinking]
passage:
Ayesha's diary. Thursday night, 10.40.
Okay, day seven of the log Bidisha dared me to keep. I just added it up on the back of a grocery list. Meetings: fine, all inside office hours. Evenings: I "worked late" on five of seven nights. But doing what? Replying to chat threads. Forty-one late replies. Actual emergencies among them: one, the payment page going down on Tuesday. One!
I've spent months feeling like a bad employee for being tired, like I was always behind on the real work. I wasn't behind. I was on call for questions nobody needed answered before breakfast.
Tomorrow I'll show Bidisha the numbers and ask her how she handles the thread noise. Weirdly, I don't feel guilty tonight. I feel annoyed, and a bit free.

qa.q: How many late replies did Ayesha count in the week?
qa.a: Forty-one late replies, with only one emergency among them: the payment page going down on Tuesday.

qa.q: What does Ayesha mean by feeling "annoyed, and a bit free"?
qa.a: The old guilt has lifted; Ayesha is annoyed at the habit of answering needless threads but relieved, because the numbers show the work was never really behind.

qa.q: Which approach could Ayesha try next with this data?
qa.a: Ayesha could agree with Bidisha to nudge each other to close the chat at a set hour, or tell the team that non-urgent threads get answered in the morning.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see the log when Ayesha shows it tomorrow?
qa.a: Bidisha will probably be glad the dare worked and may recognise the same thread noise in her own evenings 🙂

grounding: It illustrates keeping a week-long log of evening work and discovering that nearly all late hours were chat replies rather than emergencies, which dissolves vague guilt.
